After the fight in the lunch queue, Reena's friend group of five became a group of four, and Reena wasn't in it. That night she posted a single line on her status: "Some people show their true colours eventually." Then she turned her phone off.
For a week she came straight home from school in their Thane building and shut her door. She stopped going down to the courtyard.
Her older sister Arohi noticed the door and the status. On Saturday she knocked with chai.
"I saw your status. Want to tell me about it, or just drink this?"
Reena drank half the cup in silence. Then it poured out: the group chat without her, the photo from the birthday she wasn't invited to.
Arohi listened, and didn't call them worthless. She said, "That sounds so lonely."
That evening their mother took them both out for pani puri, and Reena laughed for the first time in a week.

When Francis and I broke up at sixteen, I thought I'd never feel normal again. It had been eight months, which felt like forever. He said he just wanted to focus on exams. Everyone said it was mutual. It wasn't.
For two weeks I didn't eat breakfast. I deleted every photo, then undeleted them at midnight. I posted sad lyrics with no caption. I stopped going to dance class.

I cried till I couldn't breathe properly. She just stayed.

It didn't stop hurting overnight. But I wasn't carrying it alone anymore.

The next morning, Irawati ran up at the well. "Sorry, sorry, sorry, Pooja! Please don't be angry. You know I love you!" Her voice was soft and sweet.
Pooja wondered. Irawati said sorry very quickly, every time. It was easy for her.
"Okay," Pooja said slowly. "Let's see."
Over the next weeks, Pooja watched. When they planned to study together on Sunday, Irawati came early. When her cousin invited her somewhere, she said, "I promised Pooja." She didn't make a big speech about it.
By the next fair, Pooja didn't wonder anymore. She met Irawati by the banyan tree, and Irawati was already there, waving.

qa.q: How long had Pooja waited by the banyan tree?
qa.a: For an hour.

qa.q: What was Pooja thinking when Irawati apologised so sweetly?
qa.a: Pooja felt doubtful and cautious, wondering if the quick sorry was sincere since it always came easily to Irawati.

qa.q: Which choice of Pooja's was wise, and why?
qa.a: Saying "Let's see" and watching Irawati's behaviour over weeks, because sincerity shows in actions over time, not in quick words.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt when Pooja said "Let's see"?
qa.a: Irawati may have felt a little hurt or anxious, realising she would have to show she meant it.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager reading a friend's quick, pleading sorry and judging sincerity by changed behaviour over time.

In Copenhagen, Jamal had posted a mocking picture of Astrid's drawing in the class group chat, and everyone had laughed. That evening he sent her twelve messages: "I'm so sorry." "Please forgive me." "I feel terrible."
The next day, her friends crowded round her locker. "He said sorry, Astrid. Just let it go. It's awkward for everyone."
Astrid felt the pressure squeezing her. It would be easier to smile and say fine.
But she thought about it. Jamal had also said sorry after mocking her accent in autumn, and done it again two weeks later.
When Jamal came up, pleading softly, "Please, Astrid," she said, "I hear that you're sorry. I'm not ready to forgive yet. I need to see it stop first."
Her friends went quiet. Jamal nodded, looking at the floor.
A month later, he hadn't posted anything about anyone. Astrid said hello to him in the corridor.

qa.q: How many messages did Jamal send that evening?
qa.a: He sent her twelve messages.

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling when her friends urged her to let it go?
qa.a: Astrid felt pressured and uncomfortable, tempted to smile and say fine just to end the awkwardness.

qa.q: What did Astrid do that protected her boundaries?
qa.a: She acknowledged Jamal's apology but refused to forgive on demand, asking to see the behaviour stop first.

qa.q: How might Astrid's friends have seen the situation?
qa.a: They seemed to see forgiving quickly as the easy way to end awkwardness, without thinking about Astrid's need for real change.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager reading pleading apologies, judging sincerity by changed behaviour over time, and resisting pressure to forgive.

Aditi, you look like you want to hide under the bed. Sit. Let your Omkar Ajoba tell you something.
At fourteen I copied answers in a maths test. The teacher caught me. In front of everyone.
For a week I couldn't look at anyone. I skipped school two days and said I had fever. I told myself, "I'm a cheat. I'm a bad boy." I hid from my own mother.
Then Mr Kulkarni, the teacher who caught me, came to our house. I thought I'd die of shame.
He sat with my father and said, "Omkar did a wrong thing. Omkar is not a wrong boy." Then he turned to me. "What do you want to do about it?"
Something changed. I said, "I want to take the test again. Properly." I did. I scored less, but I could look at him.
Feeling "I did bad" made me fix it. Feeling "I am bad" only made me hide.

qa.q: How many days did Omkar skip school?
qa.a: He skipped school two days and said he had fever.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling during the week after he was caught?
qa.a: He felt deep shame, believing he was a bad boy, which made him hide from everyone, even his mother.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Omkar Ajoba's story?
qa.a: Mr Kulkarni separating the act from the person and asking what Omkar wanted to do, which turned shame into guilt that led to repair.

qa.q: How might Mr Kulkarni have seen Omkar?
qa.a: He saw a boy who did something wrong but was not bad, and came to the house to help him repair it with care.

grounding: The elder's story shows the difference between shame that drives hiding and guilt that drives repair, and an adult responding to the person with care.

The principal's inspection was the next morning, and the chemistry lab was a mess. Raghav had been asked to lock it on Friday. He forgot. Now two beakers and a thermometer were missing.
Noor found him hiding in the library behind the atlas shelf.
"Everyone's looking for you."
"I'm the worst," he said. "I always mess things up. I'm useless. I can't go back there."
Noor sat down. "You forgot to lock a door. That's a thing you did. It's not what you are."
Raghav didn't answer, but he stopped pulling at his sleeve.
"What would fix it?" she asked.
He thought. "Tell Ma'am. Help her count what's missing. Maybe the cleaners moved them."
They went together. Mrs Pinto listened and said, "Thank you for coming to me, Raghav. Mistakes happen. Let's check the store." The beakers were in the store cupboard. Only the thermometer was really gone.

qa.q: What was missing from the chemistry lab?
qa.a: Two beakers and a thermometer.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling while hiding behind the atlas shelf?
qa.a: Raghav felt ashamed and useless, as if he were a bad person, which made him want to hide.

qa.q: How did Noor help turn shame into something useful?
qa.a: She separated the act from the person and asked what would fix it, which helped him move from hiding to repair.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pinto respond, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She thanked Raghav and calmly helped search, responding to him with care, which made it easier for him to face the mistake.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager's shame driving him to hide, and a friend and teacher helping it become guilt that leads to repair.

On Tuesday, in the corridor of their Delhi school, Sabina had called Noor's new haircut "a bird's nest" in front of the whole class. Noor had laughed, then gone quiet all day.
By Wednesday Sabina was avoiding Noor completely. She took a different staircase. She ate lunch in the library. At home she told her mother, "I'm a horrible person. Everyone must hate me."
Her mother put down her tea. "Did you do something unkind?"
"Yes."
"Then you did a horrible thing. That's different from being a horrible person. People who are horrible don't feel this bad."
Sabina sniffed. "So what do I do?"
"What would help Noor?"
"Say sorry. Properly. And tell the class the haircut's nice."
On Thursday Sabina found Noor at the water cooler. "The bird's nest thing. It was mean. I'm sorry." Noor smiled a little. "It was a bit mean. Thanks."

qa.q: What had Sabina called Noor's new haircut?
qa.a: "A bird's nest."

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she avoided Noor?
qa.a: Sabina felt shame, believing she was a horrible person, which drove her to hide on different staircases and in the library.

qa.q: What did Sabina's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She separated the act from the person and asked what would help Noor, which turned shame into guilt that led to a real apology.

qa.q: How might Noor have seen Sabina's avoidance before the apology?
qa.a: Noor might have thought Sabina didn't care or was still mocking her, not knowing Sabina was hiding out of shame.

grounding: The scene shows shame driving a teenager to hide, and a parent helping it become guilt that motivates repair.

Farida, you think your Wasim Nana was always this talkative? When I was fifteen, I couldn't even ask the shopkeeper for a pencil without my face going red.
In class I knew the answers, but I'd pretend I didn't. If the teacher called my name, my voice disappeared. I spent whole evenings replaying every word I'd said and thinking everyone had laughed.
My uncle noticed. He didn't force me onto a stage. He said, "One thing a day. Small."
Day one, I said "salaam" first to the milkman. Day two, I asked the price of mangoes. Week two, I read one line of poetry at a family dinner. My ears were burning, but I did it.
By the end of that year, I was reading the whole poem at the school function. Still nervous. But I could do it.
So, Farida, no stages yet. Just one small thing tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Wasim say first to the milkman?
qa.a: He said "salaam" first to the milkman.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel about speaking at fifteen?
qa.a: He felt painfully shy and self-conscious, his face going red and his voice disappearing, and he replayed his words all evening.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Wasim Nana's story?
qa.a: His uncle suggesting one small step a day, which slowly built comfort until he could read a whole poem at the school function.

qa.q: How might Wasim's uncle have seen his shyness?
qa.a: He seemed to understand it gently, choosing small steps instead of pushing Wasim onto a stage.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager's shyness and self-consciousness easing through small steps into social situations.

At his cousin's wedding in Indore, Samir had spent two hours standing against the wall, cheeks hot, sure everyone was looking at his too-big borrowed kurta.
Then the power went out in the middle of the sangeet. Screams, then laughter. Someone shouted for torches.
His aunt, Sangeeta Mami, found him in the dark. "Samir! Your phone has the best torch. Come, hold it for the dancers."
He froze. The dance floor. In front of everyone.
"You don't have to dance," she whispered. "Just stand at the edge and shine the light. That's all."
He took a breath and walked to the edge. His hand shook. But everyone was looking at the dancers, not him.
When the power came back, an uncle clapped him on the back. "Our lighting director!"
Samir laughed, surprised at himself. Later, when Mami pulled him in for the last song, he danced for half a minute before escaping, grinning.

qa.q: Where was the wedding?
qa.a: In Indore.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he stood against the wall?
qa.a: Samir felt shy and self-conscious, cheeks hot, sure everyone was judging his too-big kurta.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta Mami's idea work?
qa.a: She gave him a small, useful job at the edge of the crowd, a manageable step that didn't put him in the spotlight.

qa.q: How might the guests have seen Samir holding the torch?
qa.a: Most were watching the dancers, and those who noticed, like the uncle, saw him as helpful, not awkward.

grounding: The scene shows a self-conscious teenager taking a small step into a social situation, which builds comfort.

Lalremsiami had come from Aizawl to a Delhi school in Class 9, and for the first month she barely spoke. When anyone looked at her, she blushed and looked at her notebook. At lunch she sat at the end of the bench and read.
Shalini, who sat in front of her, noticed. She didn't drag her into a crowd. On Monday she just turned around and said, "Can I borrow your ruler? Mine broke."
On Wednesday she asked, "What's the word for 'thank you' in Mizo?"
Lalremsiami told her, very quietly. Shalini tried it and got it wrong. Lalremsiami laughed, surprised at herself.
On Friday, in geography, the teacher asked about hills in the northeast. Lalremsiami's hand went halfway up, then down. Shalini whispered, "You'd know this best."
Lalremsiami raised her hand again. Her voice was soft, but she answered. And she didn't blush for long.

qa.a: From Aizawl.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling in her first month?

In a café near their college in Pune, Vidya was telling Yusuf about her fight with her mother. Halfway through, he glanced at his phone. Then again. He nodded.
Vidya stopped. "Are you even listening?"
Yusuf looked up. "Yes! Your mum wants you to do the engineering entrance and you want to do design, and she said design isn't a real job, and you cried in the auto."
Vidya blinked. That was exactly it.
"Then why do you keep looking at your phone?"
"My bus. The last one is at seven, and the app keeps changing the time. Sorry. I should have said."
He turned the phone face down. "Go on. What did you say back to her?"
Vidya relaxed. She'd been sure he was elsewhere. His posture said one thing; his answer said another.
"I said I'd show her my portfolio."
"Good. Do that."

qa.q: When was Yusuf's last bus?
qa.a: The last one is at seven.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when Yusuf glanced at his phone?
qa.a: Vidya felt hurt and unheard, sure he wasn't listening to something important.

qa.q: What checked whether Yusuf was really listening?
qa.a: Vidya's brief question, "Are you even listening?", which showed he had heard every detail despite looking at his phone.

qa.q: How did Yusuf see his phone glances?
qa.a: He saw them as checking the bus time, not as ignoring Vidya, though he realised he should have said so.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager nodding while glancing at a phone, and a brief question revealing he was actually listening.

Last Sunday my father, Nitin, sat down next to me on the sofa and started talking about summer courses. Coding camp, art camp, maybe a language. I nodded along. I said "mm" a lot. I was scrolling through photos of my friend's party on my phone.
After a while he stopped and said, calmly, "Kalyani, which one did you like?"
I looked up. I had no idea what he'd said. My face went hot.
"Sorry, Papa. I wasn't listening."
He didn't get angry. He said, "You were nodding. I thought you were."
That stuck with me. My nodding had fooled both of us.
I put the phone in the other room, and we went through the list again. I actually liked the language course.
Now when I notice myself nodding on autopilot, I ask myself what the person just said. If I can't answer, I put the phone away.

qa.q: What was Kalyani scrolling through?
qa.a: Photos of a friend's party.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she couldn't answer Papa's question?
qa.a: Kalyani felt embarrassed and a little guilty, her face going hot, realising the nodding had hidden a lack of listening.

qa.q: What small habit did Kalyani take from this?
qa.a: Checking silently what the person just said when nodding on autopilot, and putting the phone away if no answer comes.

qa.q: How did Nitin read Kalyani's nodding?
qa.a: He took the nodding as a sign of listening, until a brief question showed it wasn't.
